# Ed McMahon, Beloved TV Sidekick and Announcer, Dies at 86

Ed McMahon, the genial announcer and second banana whose booming "Heeeere's Johnny!" introduced Johnny Carson to millions of "Tonight Show" viewers for three decades, has died. He was 86.

McMahon died early Tuesday at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center in Los Angeles, surrounded by family, according to his publicist Howard Bragman. He had battled a variety of health issues in recent years, including pneumonia and bone cancer.

For 30 years, McMahon served as the perfect complement to Carson on "The Tonight Show," his hearty laugh and warm presence helping to establish one of the most successful partnerships in television history. Beyond his role as sidekick, McMahon hosted "Star Search," co-hosted "TV's Bloopers & Practical Jokes" with Dick Clark, and became a familiar face pitching everything from dog food to sweepstakes.

## An Enduring Partnership

McMahon and Carson first worked together on the game show "Who Do You Trust?" before moving to "The Tonight Show" in 1962. Their on-air chemistry became the stuff of television legend, with McMahon serving as the ideal foil for Carson's comedic timing.

The pair remained close until Carson's death in 2005.

## Tributes Pour In

News of McMahon's death prompted an outpouring of grief from friends and colleagues across the entertainment world.

**David Letterman**, who considered Carson and McMahon influences on his own career, reflected on McMahon's talent. "Ed McMahon was the greatest," Letterman said. "For those of us who grew up watching him, he made it look effortless. He was the definition of a class act, and there will never be another one like him."

**Joan Rivers**, a frequent "Tonight Show" guest and guest host, remembered McMahon's warmth. "Ed was one of the sweetest men in the business," Rivers said. "He always made you feel welcome, always had that wonderful laugh. Backstage, he treated everyone the same, whether you were a star or a stagehand. I adored him."

**Dick Clark**, McMahon's co-host on "TV's Bloopers & Practical Jokes," spoke of their years working together. "Ed was a joy to work with, a true professional and an even better friend," Clark said. "We shared so many laughs over the years. He had a generosity of spirit that came through in everything he did. I'll miss him terribly."

**Doc Severinsen**, the "Tonight Show" bandleader who shared the stage with McMahon for decades, called him irreplaceable. "Ed was family," Severinsen said. "Night after night, year after year, we were all part of something special, and Ed was at the heart of it. His laugh could fill a room. My heart is broken."

**Don Rickles**, the legendary insult comic and longtime friend, offered a characteristically affectionate remembrance. "Ed McMahon was a big, wonderful teddy bear of a man," Rickles said. "I gave him a hard time for years, and he took it all with that great laugh of his. The truth is, I loved the guy. Television lost a giant today, and I lost a dear friend."

## A Life Beyond the Desk

Born Edward Leo Peter McMahon Jr. on March 6, 1923, in Detroit, McMahon served as a Marine Corps fighter pilot during World War II and later flew missions in the Korean War, earning several decorations. His military service remained a source of great pride throughout his life.

After the war, McMahon worked in early television before his fateful pairing with Carson. His career spanned more than half a century, making him one of the most recognizable voices and faces in American broadcasting.

In his later years, McMahon faced well-publicized financial difficulties and health struggles, matters he addressed with characteristic candor and humor.

McMahon is survived by his wife, Pamela, and his children.

He will be remembered as the man who, night after night, welcomed America into its living rooms with a smile and that unmistakable, joyous laugh.

*A tribute to the man who made supporting brilliant*

For nearly three decades, American television audiences settled into their evenings with two familiar voices. One belonged to Johnny Carson, the mercurial king of late-night comedy. The other—warm, booming, and unmistakable—belonged to Ed McMahon, the man who transformed the humble role of the television sidekick into an art form all its own.

McMahon's legendary introduction became one of the most recognized phrases in broadcasting history, but reducing his contribution to that iconic four-word announcement misses the depth of what he brought to "The Tonight Show." From 1962 to 1992, McMahon demonstrated that the sidekick was not a lesser role, but an essential one—the steady foundation upon which comedic magic could be built.

What made McMahon exceptional was his understanding that his job was to make Carson shine. His hearty laugh—sometimes criticized, often imitated—served a crucial purpose. It gave viewers permission to enjoy, signaled the rhythm of a joke, and provided Carson with a responsive partner who elevated every exchange.

"The best straight man in the business," colleagues often called him, and the description fit. McMahon possessed an intuitive sense of timing, knowing precisely when to interject, when to feed a line, and when to simply step back and let his partner command the spotlight.

The magic of the Carson-McMahon partnership lay in its authenticity. Their rapport, developed over thousands of broadcasts, created a comfortable intimacy that drew viewers in night after night. McMahon could banter with ease during the opening monologue, play along in comedy sketches like the beloved "Carnac the Magnificent," and gracefully anchor the desk during interviews.

This was no accident of casting. McMahon brought a broadcaster's professionalism and a performer's instinct, understanding that great support requires as much skill as headlining—perhaps more, because it demands ego be set aside in service of the whole.

## The Template for Generations

McMahon's influence extended far beyond his own tenure. He essentially wrote the playbook for the modern television sidekick, demonstrating that the role could carry genuine cultural weight. Every announcer, every co-host, every second-in-command who followed owed something to the standard he established.

He proved that a sidekick could become a beloved institution in his own right—a familiar friend welcomed into millions of homes, whose presence signaled comfort, reliability, and good humor.

## An Enduring Legacy

When McMahon and Carson said their final goodbyes in May 1992, television lost one of its greatest partnerships. But Ed McMahon's contribution to the medium remains permanent. He elevated a supporting role into something noble, showing that there is profound artistry in making others look their best.

In an industry that often celebrates the spotlight, Ed McMahon reminded us of the quiet power of the perfect complement—the reliable presence, the generous laugh, the steady hand that helped make legendary television possible.

He was, in every sense, the definitive sidekick. And American television was richer for it.

# The Art of the Second Banana: Remembering Ed McMahon and the Comedy of Selfless Support

When Ed McMahon passed away in 2009 at the age of 86, television lost more than a familiar face and a booming voice. It lost one of the finest practitioners of a peculiar and underappreciated craft: the art of being a "second banana." For nearly thirty years, McMahon sat to the right of Johnny Carson on *The Tonight Show*, and in doing so, he defined what it means to be the perfect comedic partner—the one who doesn't get the biggest laugh, but who makes the biggest laugh possible.

## What Is a "Second Banana"?

The term "second banana" originated in the world of burlesque and vaudeville, where the top comedian was the "top banana" and his supporting comic was the "second banana." The phrase reportedly derives from an old comedy routine involving a bunch of bananas being passed around, with the lead comic keeping the largest for himself.

But the second banana is far more than a mere sidekick or straight man. A great second banana is a comedic instrument—someone who understands rhythm, timing, and the delicate ecosystem of a joke. They know precisely when to laugh, when to feign offense, when to prod their partner toward the punchline, and, most crucially, when to disappear entirely. The second banana's ego must be subordinate to the comedy itself.

## The Perfect Setup Man

Ed McMahon was, by nearly universal acclaim, the gold standard of this profession. His most famous contribution was deceptively simple: the thunderous introduction, "Heeeeere's Johnny!" These two words, delivered nightly with unwavering enthusiasm, became one of the most recognizable phrases in American television history. Yet notice what McMahon accomplished with them—he built the anticipation, threw open the curtain, and then stepped aside to let Carson shine.

This was the essence of his genius. During Carson's opening monologues, McMahon served as a human laugh track and safety net rolled into one. When a joke landed, his hearty laugh amplified the audience's response. When a joke fell flat—as jokes inevitably do—McMahon's reaction became the salvage operation. Carson would turn to him, and the two would mine comedy gold from the very failure of the joke. McMahon's presence transformed a bombed punchline into a shared moment of improvisation, often funnier than the original material would have been.

## The Chemistry of Two

What made the Carson-McMahon partnership legendary was not that McMahon competed with Carson, but that he completed him. Carson was the cool, quick-witted center of the show; McMahon was the warm, hearty foil. Carson could raise a single eyebrow at one of McMahon's overly enthusiastic laughs or gently mock his sidekick's reputation for enjoying a cocktail, and McMahon would absorb these jabs with genial good humor, giving as good as he got when the moment called for it.
